set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described mostly in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later; the one general-population test read here, for alcohol, did not find the full pattern; and a US general-population survey of cannabis use disorder, not read here, is described as finding a shorter course in women. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among the 38,309 lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks ever), men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age). The authors read these hazards, the survival curves and a significant interaction of cohort, gender and time (its estimates not shown) as men becoming dependent faster, especially in younger cohorts. In the editors' reading, a hazard among all drinkers combines the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, and because the average times below were similar, the higher hazard in men mostly reflects that more men became dependent (in the table's unweighted counts, 23.7% of male and 16.2% of female lifetime drinkers; editors' arithmetic). Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted); it was shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years) and, not marked significant, in those born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4), and longer, not significantly, in women of the other three cohorts. Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the phrase 'telescoped development' was first used in 1958; the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term asked 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups to recall four landmark ages, and the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter on average in the women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids, but not heroin, found mainly in women already in treatment, and, following an earlier review, explains the difference from population surveys by who is sampled: women in treatment likely have more severe disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; its cannabis citation points to a general-population paper on alcohol dependence). The same group's earlier review states as established that women advance faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies, among them treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996) that the review itself describes elsewhere as showing no earlier treatment entry for women (Greenfield et al., 2007). Randall et al. (1999), a treatment-sample study that the papers read describe in opposite ways, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men? This has not been shown for women in general. The idea, called 'telescoping', came mostly from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened, and its stages were first drawn from men's stories. In two big US surveys of adults in the general population, women had their first drink later than men, and fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Among the people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men, on average about 6 years after their first drink, and a little faster in one age group. The survey's authors read their results as men getting there faster; the editors think this mostly shows that more men became dependent. A US survey about cannabis, known here only from another paper's short description, found a faster course in women. A review suggests that the women who reach treatment may have more severe problems, which would explain why a faster course shows up in treatment. All these studies relied on memory. See the contested question.
set.population: Adults in two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002; US-born, aged 18 to 57; 53,238 people, 38,309 of whom were lifetime drinkers, with more than 12 drinks ever) for alcohol; for other drugs and for treatment and self-help samples, studies described in a historical critique and two narrative reviews, among them one general-population survey of cannabis use disorder
set.magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks), men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed, read by the authors as faster progression in men; whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); share of lifetime drinkers with a time to dependence in the unweighted Table 1 counts, men 23.7% vs women 16.2% (4,631 of 19,549 and 3,121 of 19,263; editors' arithmetic; these counts total 7,752, against 8,564 people with dependence in the hazard analysis); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card), and longer in women in the other three cohorts (3.1 vs 2.8, 8.6 vs 7.9 and 11.8 vs 10.4 years; none marked significant); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): the 1989 study credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; 75 of 103 citing articles used the 1989 study as background. General-population survey of cannabis use disorder, second-hand (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018; NESARC by its reference title; 1,217 women, 3,297 men): first use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, timing measure and adjustment not given.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Every timing was recalled at a single interview or in questionnaires, years or decades later (card sc_keyes_2010: JBI, moderate); treatment samples select people by having reached treatment and are known here only through reviews that did not appraise them (cards sc_marks_2018, sc_mchugh_2018, sc_greenfield_2007); in the survey analysis the hazards among all drinkers mix the chance of dependence with its speed, the averages among people who became dependent are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently, and several table and text values disagree.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Treatment samples, and one general-population cannabis survey known only second-hand, point towards a faster course in women, while the general-population alcohol analysis does not; within the survey paper, the hazards (read by the authors as men faster) and the averages among people who became dependent (no difference overall; women faster in one cohort) differ; a review, following an earlier one, explains the difference by sample, which is plausible but untested.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: The only general-population test read concerns alcohol, in US-born adults aged 18 to 57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002; the evidence for other drugs, including the general-population cannabis survey, and from treatment samples is second-hand (narrative reviews; METHODS §6.3).
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The survey estimates are precise (at least 4,603 people per cohort); the small treatment samples (33 women in the 1989 study) are part of the second-hand evidence already rated down.
set.grade.domains.publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that 75 of 103 papers citing the 1989 study used it without testing it concerns citation, not publication.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) by the same group and reuses its search; both reviews and the critique describe overlapping treatment-sample studies and the same general-population analysis (Keyes et al., 2010), so they add no independent data; the survey analysis pools NLAES, which Greenfield et al. also cite through Dawson (1996), and NESARC, which is also the source of the cannabis analysis (Khan et al., 2013) that Marks & Clark describe. Each figure is labelled with its quantity: hazards among all drinkers (chance and speed together, read by the authors as speed) or averages among people who reached the step (speed only); that the hazards mostly reflect the chance of becoming dependent is the editors' reading, resting on the similar average times and on Table 1's unweighted counts, and the claim gives the authors' reading beside it. Randall et al. (1999), a treatment-sample study, is not yet read and is described in opposite ways by the papers read; reading it, and Khan et al. (2013) for cannabis, could change the yes side. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways (treatment samples and a second-hand general-population cannabis survey against the general-population alcohol survey), with a published critique of the concept, so the six-part debate box applies.
set.debate.evidence_yes: The faster course was described mostly in people in treatment. In the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups recalled their landmark ages: the women had started drinking about 2 years later and had first been drunk about 3 years later, entered treatment at the same age, and went from their first alcohol-related problem to their first treatment 4.3 years faster on average; in an earlier Iowa treatment sample (3,132 men and 395 women), women reached treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit and men about 3 (as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). A US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) is described as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, which is evidence from outside treatment; its timing measure and adjustment are not given and it is not read here (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids (McHugh et al., 2018), and the same group's earlier review states faster progression to first treatment as established for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (Greenfield et al., 2007). In the general-population alcohol surveys, among the people who did become dependent, women born 1964–1973 got there faster than men (on average 3.7 against 4.2 years), the printed figures suggest the same for women born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4 years, not marked significant; an editors' approximation on the study card), and among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010).
set.debate.evidence_no: In the only general-population test read, two pooled US national surveys (1991–1992 and 2001–2002; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57), women started drinking later than men, but among the lifetime drinkers men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every birth cohort (1.36 to 1.79) and, among people with dependence, a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in two of five cohorts, 1.55 and 1.42), after adjustment for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink (and, by the table's footnote, age); the authors read the dependence hazards as men progressing faster, especially in younger cohorts. Among people who became dependent, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years) and, in three of five cohorts, longer in women, not significantly; the authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population (Keyes et al., 2010). A narrative review, following an earlier one, explains the gap between treatment samples and population surveys by who is sampled, since women who reach treatment likely have more severe disorders, and reports that telescoping was not found for heroin (McHugh et al., 2018). The historical critique shows that the stages that define telescoping were drawn from the recalled histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed, 15 women's answers set aside), that the 1989 study was small and drawn from treatment and self-help settings, and that 75 of 103 papers citing it used it as background without testing it; it argues that, with women as the reference group, men's longer course might have been called magnification, and recommends discarding the term (Marks & Clark, 2018).
set.debate.neither_can_show: Every timing in these studies was recalled, often decades later, at a single interview or in a questionnaire; none was recorded as it happened, and no study read tested whether women and men remember timing differently (the surveys' recall check, which the authors read as showing limited recall bias, tested only whether dependence beginning at 25 or later was reported less often by members of the same birth cohorts interviewed 10 years later). Treatment samples time only people who reached treatment, so a group that reaches treatment soon after its problems begin will look fast whatever its course in the population. In the general-population surveys, hazards among all drinkers combine the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, so on their own they cannot say who is faster; the averages among people who became dependent come closer to speed but are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and the youngest cohort, interviewed only as young adults, could contribute only early steps. People who died before the surveys, or were older than 57, are missing. None of these designs separates sex (biology) from gender (roles, access to treatment, stigma); the general-population evidence read is for alcohol in the USA only, and the cannabis survey is known only from a short description in another paper.
set.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The faster course in women was described mostly in small treatment and self-help samples, from recalled ages, and the idea grew out of stage models built from men's recalled histories. In the one general-population test read, for alcohol in the USA, women were less likely than men to become dependent and, once dependent, had a lower hazard of reaching treatment, and those who did become dependent got there about as fast as men on average, faster in one birth cohort; the authors read the same data as men progressing faster, a reading that rests on hazards that mix the chance of dependence with its speed and on an interaction whose estimates are not shown. So the evidence read here does not show that women in general move faster from first use to dependence; whether women who do develop dependence move faster, and whether this holds for other drugs, is open. The studies that bear most directly on the yes side, Randall et al. (1999) for alcohol in a treatment sample and Khan et al. (2013) for cannabis in a general-population survey, are known here only from other papers' descriptions, which disagree about the first.

evidence_set: The three-way interaction of cohort, gender and time for time to dependence was significant (F=54.08 in the text, 54.1 in Table 2; df 6; p<0.01); its estimates are not shown, and the authors describe its direction as men having a shorter time from first drink to dependence than women, and than men in earlier cohorts, in more recent cohorts, consistent with the survival curves; the abstract's statement that men progress faster, especially in younger cohorts, cannot be checked from the numbers printed.

The authors locate gender bias in the progressive-disease conventions drawn from convenience samples of mostly male members of Alcoholics Anonymous (a point they attribute to other scholars), which leave out people who recover without treatment; in landmarks, criteria and instruments validated in men, with men as the reference group (with women as the reference, men's longer course might have been called magnification); and in comparative wording such as accelerated progression.

As summarized in the Introduction: for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, women advance faster than men from use to regular use to first treatment and arrive with equal severity after fewer years of use, stated as established and cited to six studies, among them treatment samples (Piazza et al., 1989; Randall et al., 1999; Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004) and Dawson (1996), a population survey whose results as the same review describes them in section 2.3 do not show earlier treatment entry for women (study card reporting issue); the label of a most reproducible finding belongs to the sentence before, on women's vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences, not to faster progression; no sample type, timing measure or adjustment is described.

set.statement: In US national household surveys, women with alcohol dependence compared with men with alcohol dependence were less likely, or slower, to reach alcohol treatment in the years after their problems began, while for drug use disorders, and for treatment in the past year, no gender difference was described; treatment was uncommon for both. Some studies described by a review found that the women who did reach treatment got there sooner after first use or onset, which concerns speed among people treated, not who gets treatment. In two pooled general-population surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, and NESARC, 2001–2002; 8,564 US-born adults aged 18 to 57 with alcohol dependence, not counting 258 first treated before dependence began; ages at onset and at first treatment recalled at a single interview), the hazard of first alcohol treatment was higher in men than in women in all five birth cohorts, significantly in people born 1954–1963 (hazard ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.73) and 1964–1973 (1.55, 1.22 to 1.96), with intervals including no difference in the other three, and over all cohorts together the difference was significant (F = 22.7, p < 0.001); the models adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age; about a quarter (24.6%) of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment; among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010). As described by a narrative review, an earlier analysis of the 1991–1992 survey (Dawson, 1996; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; onset and treatment reported after the fact; adjustment not described) found that 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (counting a doctor, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, another professional or a treatment facility), with no gender difference in the first 8 years after onset, men 13% to 20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset, and no difference among the most severely dependent; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence was 12.5% in women and 12.1% in men in a 1999 household survey, and gender was not associated with past-year use of substance use services in the 2002 national survey (Greenfield et al., 2007, second-hand). Women were a smaller share of people in US alcohol treatment than of people with alcohol use disorders (men to women 3.3 to 1 in treatment facilities against 2.7 to 1 in the population in 1991), and women with drinking problems more often sought help in mental-health and other non-specialist services; barriers described for women include childcare, pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, stigma and co-occurring mental-health problems (Greenfield et al., 2007). A later review reports, from the 2015 national survey, that 10.4% of women and 11.1% of men who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, that under-treatment was most marked among women with alcohol use disorder, that gender was not associated with past-year treatment use for illicit drug use disorders, and that some studies found women reached treatment sooner after first use and after onset; it adds that women with alcohol use disorder more often named stigma as a barrier in two population surveys, while other surveys found few gender differences in barriers, perhaps because they did not ask about pregnancy, childcare or family attitudes (McHugh et al., 2018, second-hand). The two analyses of the 1991–1992 survey share data and are not independent; all timing and treatment were self-reported, years later; 'treatment' was defined differently across studies; and the figures are from the USA. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two analyses that share a survey).
set.plain: Are women less likely than men to get treatment? For alcohol, somewhat. In US surveys, men with alcohol dependence reached treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups. In one 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated, and the gap appeared only 8 or more years after the problems began. Some studies found that the women who did get treatment got there sooner after their problems began. For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, the reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment for alcohol or drugs got it. Women more often went to mental-health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences between women and men in the barriers they named, apart from stigma. People reported all of this themselves, years later, and the figures are from the US.

set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women and men who enter treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders differ in how long they stay or how well they do: as summarized by two narrative reviews from one research group, most large studies found no gender difference in retention, completion or outcome; where differences appeared, the 2007 review found that they generally favoured women, while most of the differences the 2018 update lists, for quitting smoking and for particular medicines, went against women; the reviews' figures are second-hand. A review of 280 articles published from 1975 to 2005 (11.8% of them randomized trials; the studies were not appraised) describes large multi-programme data sets with very few gender differences in retention (among 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; in a national study of 4,689 adults, gender was not associated with completion after adjustment), small clinical studies that disagreed (five found women more likely to drop out, two less likely), and outcome studies that mostly found no difference and, where they found one, mostly favoured women (in one study of older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women and 54% of men were abstinent at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjustment for length of stay, although the women still reported no heavy-drinking days in the past month against an average of four among the men) (Greenfield et al., 2007). The group's 2018 update describes no gender difference in outcome in large randomized trials (COMBINE, 1,226 people with alcohol dependence, 31% women; a prescription-opioid trial, 653 people, 40% women), none in retention across 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (more than 11,000 people), and none in completion across more than 1.7 million US treatment episodes, except that women less often completed detoxification; behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups showed no clear difference between women and men. The exceptions it lists mostly go against women: worse results in quitting smoking, nicotine replacement working better in men, and worse responses in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence and to buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (where buspirone did no better than placebo in either sex); one smoking medicine, varenicline, worked better in women in one meta-analysis and gave women more benefit than other aids in another, naltrexone findings for alcohol were mixed, and the effect of disulfiram for alcohol dependence in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants (McHugh et al., 2018). Comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment were few and mixed. Of the randomized comparisons described in the 2007 review, one found no difference in early dropout, one found better retention in a women-only day programme, and in the one that compared alcohol and drug outcomes the women-only day programme did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes and had lower abstinence than a hospital programme that cost twice as much per week; the review concludes that women may be equally well served by good programmes of either kind and that changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes (Greenfield et al., 2007). The 2018 update describes comparisons in which women in women-only programmes did better (across 43 programmes, despite greater severity; and on later crime and incarceration, designs not described), randomized trials it cites as supporting programmes designed for particular groups of women (women with children, with co-occurring psychiatric disorders or in the criminal justice system), and two trials of the group's own women's group therapy: better than mixed-gender group counselling at 6 months in a small first trial, and as effective, not more, in a larger one (McHugh et al., 2018). These comparisons are between women and men who had already entered treatment; within trials, women and men were compared as subgroups, not assigned at random; outcomes were defined in many different ways; a non-significant difference is not evidence that outcomes are the same; and several of the analyses are the reviewers' own. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Once in treatment, do women do as well as men? Most large studies found no difference: women and men stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Where differences did appear, the older review found that women mostly did better, while the newer one listed more results in which women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines. Programmes for women only gave mixed results: in the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones and did less well than a costlier hospital programme, and some other studies favoured women-only programmes. All of this comes from two reviews by one research group, which did not check the quality of the studies, and finding no difference is not proof that results are the same.
set.magnitude: Second-hand, none pooled, mostly without intervals. Greenfield et al. (2007): 280 articles 1975–2005, 11.8% randomized trials; small clinical retention studies, five with more dropout in women, two with less, one mixed; 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more often completed where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults, abstinence in the past 30 days at 6 months 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay, heavy-drinking days in the past month none in women vs an average of four in men; randomized comparison of outcomes in women-only against mixed-gender day programmes, women-only no different from two community programmes, lower total abstinence than a hospital programme costing twice as much per week. McHugh et al. (2018): COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women), no gender difference in outcome; 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000), no difference in retention; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes, no difference in completion except detoxification (women less often); smoking cessation worse in women; nicotine replacement better in men; varenicline better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (n = 14,389, 51% women), comparable against placebo with more benefit for women relative to other aids; disulfiram for cocaine dependence and buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence worse in women; naltrexone for alcohol mixed; women 1.2% of participants in the disulfiram trials for alcohol cited as an example; women in women-only programmes better on drug use across 43 programmes (observational).
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The large studies agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome. The differences found point both ways and differ by era and treatment (programmes and psychosocial treatment in the 2007 review, mostly favouring women where present; quitting smoking and particular medicines in the 2018 update, mostly against women), which the claim states; small clinical studies of retention split five to two against women.
set.grade.reasoning: The studies described are mostly observational, and even in the trials gender is an observed subgroup, so the evidence starts low; down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rests only on narrative reviews: stays at draft, its figures are second-hand, and it is not for the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) with the same search terms and authors. Status replicated: as described, several independent large data sets and trials (multi-programme data sets, the Alcohol and Drug Services Study, COMBINE, a prescription-opioid trial, 24 Clinical Trials Network trials, 1.7 million treatment episodes) agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome; the specific differences point both ways and differ by era and treatment, which the claim states rather than summarizing them as favouring women; the relation is insufficient evidence because no difference was shown to be small.

evidence_add.extracted: As summarized (Kaskutas et al., 2005): women were randomized to a women-only day programme with gender-specific content or to one of three mixed-gender day programmes (two community-based, one hospital-based); the only significant outcome differences were between the women-only and the hospital-based programme, which had higher total abstinence during follow-up and cost twice as much per week, so the women-only programme did not differ from the two community-based programmes; the sample was small; the review concludes that women may be equally well served by high-quality mixed-gender and women-only day programmes.

evidence_add.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence_add.extracted: As summarized: nicotine dependence is the exception to the pattern of no gender difference, with worse outcomes in women; nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study; varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (14,389 people, 51% women), as well in both sexes against placebo but with greater benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; with naltrexone for smoking, men reduced smoking more and women gained less weight. For other medicines, gender differences were not consistently shown: women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence; trials of disulfiram for alcohol dependence report no such difference, perhaps because women were badly under-represented (for example 1.2%); naltrexone for alcohol dependence gave mixed findings (men better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, where buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.
